title: UAE, Saudi Arabia to add up to 3GW of data centre power by 2030
source_used: Khaleej Times (pool link, fetched text); the same figures checked in a Zawya copy on TradingView
key_facts: S&P Global Ratings, a credit rating agency, expects the UAE and Saudi Arabia to add about 2 to 3 gigawatts of IT power to the Middle East data center market by 2030.
That is less than 2% of global additions over 2026 to 2030; the US and Canada are expected to supply about 70% of new capacity.
The two countries are expected to account for more than 80% of the Gulf (GCC) region's data center capacity by 2030, citing the 451 Research database as of the first quarter of 2026.

Larger projects could push the numbers higher: the 5-gigawatt Stargate UAE campus in Abu Dhabi (G42, OpenAI, Nvidia, Oracle, Cisco and SoftBank), whose first 1 gigawatt is due within three years, and Saudi Humain projects of up to 1.9 gigawatts by 2030.
The UAE is speeding up its expansion while Saudi capacity additions will likely come later in the decade.
Build costs for 2026 to 2030 average about $11 million per megawatt in the UAE and $13 million in Saudi Arabia, against $12 million in Europe and $13 million in North America (451 Research).
S&P says low energy prices are a competitive advantage, the UAE is investing heavily in nuclear power, and data localisation rules and sovereign cloud policies raise demand for domestic data centers.
quote_evidence: The UAE, along with Saudi Arabia, are expected to quickly increase data centre capacity, and will account for more than 80 per cent of the region’s share of data centre capacity by 2030, as per an S&P report.
Over the next four years, the US and Canada are expected to contribute the most, at 70 per cent of new data centre capacity.
New large-scale projects, such as the 5GW Stargate UAE campus, could push these numbers even higher.
why_it_matters_hint: A rating agency projects the Gulf will stay small in global data center growth but that the UAE and Saudi Arabia will dominate the region.
event_date: S&P report reported on 5 Oct 2026; the forecast covers 2026 to 2030.
notes: An analyst projection, not a result. The S&P report itself was not opened. Khaleej Times has a typo in one sentence ('making up up less than 2 per cent'); the Zawya copy confirms the figure as less than 2 percent of global IT power additions over 2026-2030.
